title: Half of the binary digits of Champernowne's constant are 1
credit: Open question recorded by V. Becher and N. Graus; constant due to D. G. Champernowne (1933).
premise_risks: Numerical frequency at 3×10^5 bits is 0.4978, slightly below 1/2; convergence may be very slow (or, in principle, the claim false) - the problem is honest either way, but a disproof would be extremely surprising
Low novelty: normality of classical constants in other bases is a well-known folklore question
plain: Champernowne's constant C = 0.123456789101112... (write the positive integers one after another in decimal) was proved normal in base 10 in 1933: every block of decimal digits appears with the expected frequency. Nothing is known about its expansion in bases that are not powers of 10. Prove the first instance: in the binary expansion of C, the proportion of 1s among the first N digits tends to 1/2.
math: Let $C=\sum_{k\ge1}d_k10^{-k}$ where $d_1d_2d_3\ldots=123456789101112\ldots$ is the concatenation of the decimal representations of $1,2,3,\ldots$, and let $b_n=\lfloor 2^nC\rfloor\bmod 2$ for $n\ge1$. Prove that $\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\#\{1\le n\le N:\ b_n=1\}=\frac12$.
